meta.title: The Orator's Sealed Archive
meta.unit: Persuasive writing & rhetoric — ethos, pathos, logos and rhetorical devices
meta.subject: English: Language & Literature
meta.author: ISH English

story.intro: You are sealed inside the old debating society's archive, where the speeches of history's great persuaders are kept. The night warden has gone and the door has clicked shut. Each cabinet guards a secret of rhetoric; unlock them in turn to release the final bolt and step back into the corridor.
story.outro: The final bolt slides free. You have decoded the orator's craft — appeal, device, and design — and proved you can name the tools that move an audience. The archive door swings open and the corridor lights flicker on. You read the architecture of persuasion and earned your way out.

stations.name: The Mirror Plate
stations.narrative: A brass cabinet bears one word, but every letter is engraved back-to-front, as if read in a mirror.

content.prompt: Read the mirrored word the right way round to name the appeal it labels.

hints: The word has simply been written backwards — read it from right to left.
Reverse the order of the letters and a familiar rhetorical term appears.
It is the appeal to trust and character — it ends in '-thos' and begins with 'e'.
stations.reveal: Correct — ETHOS. This is the appeal to the speaker's credibility and character: we believe people we judge to be trustworthy and qualified.

stations.name: The Scattered Seal
stations.narrative: A wax seal has cracked and its carved letters have tumbled into a heap on the reading desk.

content.clue: The appeal to the audience's emotions — pity, anger, pride, fear.

hints: The clue points to the appeal that targets feelings, not logic.
Six letters; it sits beside ethos and logos as the third classical appeal.
Re-arrange the letters to spell PATHOS.
stations.reveal: PATHOS — the appeal to emotion. Persuaders use vivid imagery, anecdotes and loaded words to stir how an audience feels.

stations.name: The Misfiled Drawer
stations.narrative: Four index cards have been filed together, but one device does not belong with the rest.

content.prompt: Three of these are persuasive or rhetorical techniques. Which card has been misfiled because it does NOT belong with them?

hints: Three cards are tools a speaker uses to persuade an audience.
One card is a sound device from poetry, not a way of winning over a reader.
'Buzz', 'crash' and 'hiss' are examples of the odd one out.
stations.reveal: ONOMATOPOEIA is the odd one out — it imitates sounds and belongs to poetic sound devices. Rhetorical question, rule of three and direct address are all persuasive techniques.

stations.name: The Speaker's Plaque
stations.narrative: A brass plaque engraves a line from one of history's most famous persuasive speeches. Name who delivered it.

content.quote: I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the colour of their skin but by the content of their character.

hints: The speech was delivered during the American civil rights movement in 1963.
The repeated phrase 'I have a dream' is one of the most famous uses of anaphora in English.
The speaker shares his name with a major US public holiday in January.
stations.reveal: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered these words in 1963. The repetition of 'I have a dream' is anaphora — a rhetorical device that builds rhythm and emotional momentum (pathos) while his moral authority supplies ethos.

stations.name: The Final Manuscript
stations.narrative: The last cabinet holds a short persuasive paragraph. Read it closely; the bolt releases only for the reader who can judge how it works.

content.passage: Think of the river behind our school. Think of the children who once swam there, and the herons that once fished its banks. Today it is choked with plastic. We can clean it — but only if we act now, together, before another summer is lost.
content.question: Which technique is the writer relying on MOST to persuade the reader?
options: presenting balanced statistics from both sides
appealing to emotion through vivid images and urgency

stations.answer: appealing to emotion through vivid images and urgency
acceptedAnswers: appealing to emotion through vivid images and urgency
hints: Notice the pictures the writer paints — swimming children, fishing herons, a choked river.
There are no statistics or named experts here; the power comes from feeling and a sense of 'act now'.
This is pathos — the appeal to emotion — built from vivid imagery and urgency.
stations.reveal: Correct — the paragraph leans on pathos: vivid emotive imagery ('children who once swam', 'herons that once fished') and urgency ('act now', 'before another summer is lost') rather than data or expert testimony. Recognising which appeal dominates is how you evaluate a persuasive text.
